title: Propagation of Sound Waves
tagline: Production and propagation, wavelength, echo, reverberation and the audible range

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed by scripts/verify-math.mjs. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and needs a material medium through which to travel. Everything else in this chapter follows from that one requirement: because sound is a mechanical wave it cannot cross a vacuum, and because it needs particles to push against its speed depends on how tightly those particles are packed, which is why sound travels much faster in a solid than in air. The wave description, wavelength, frequency and amplitude, then explains pitch and loudness, and the ideas of echo and reverberation follow from the time sound takes to return.

facts.label: Key formula
facts.value: v = f lambda, speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength

facts.label: Speed in air
facts.value: About 330 to 344 metres per second at ordinary room temperature

facts.label: Audible range
facts.value: 20 Hz to 20000 Hz for the average human ear

facts.label: Echo
facts.value: A distinct reflection heard when the time gap is at least 0.1 second, needing a distance of about 17.2 m

blocks.text: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies. A vibrating object sets the particles of the surrounding medium into vibration, and those particles push and pull the neighbouring particles, which pass the disturbance on. The energy travels through the medium while the particles themselves oscillate about fixed positions and do not travel with the wave.

items: A sound wave is a longitudinal wave, in which the particles vibrate along the direction of propagation.
A medium is essential; sound cannot travel through a vacuum, so a bell cannot be heard inside a space where the air has been pumped out.
Sound travels fastest through a solid, less quickly through a liquid, and slowest through a gas, because the particles are most closely packed in a solid.
Sound needs a material medium but light does not, which is why sunlight reaches us through the vacuum of space while sound from an explosion on the Moon cannot.
The speed of sound in air is about 330 to 344 metres per second at ordinary temperature and decreases as the temperature falls.

items.text: Explain why a sound cannot be heard inside a bell jar from which the air has been evacuated.
items.note: Sound requires particles to transmit the vibration. Once the air has been pumped out there are almost no particles left to carry the disturbance, so the bell jar acts as a partial vacuum and no sound reaches the observer. A ringing bell inside the jar can still be seen vibrating, and a candle inside can be stirred, so the demonstration shows specifically that sound and not vibration needs the medium.

learn.title: Wavelength, frequency, amplitude and v = f lambda

blocks.text: A sound wave is described by three quantities. The wavelength is the distance between two consecutive compressions, or between two consecutive rarefactions. The frequency is the number of oscillations made by the source in one second. The amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its mean position, and it determines the loudness.

items.meaning: The distance between two consecutive points in phase, such as two adjacent compressions, measured in metres and denoted by lambda.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz, where 1 Hz is one cycle per second.
The maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position. A larger amplitude gives a louder sound.
The sensation determined by frequency. A high frequency gives a high pitch, a low frequency a low pitch.

items: v = f lambda, so wavelength equals speed divided by frequency.
For a given medium the speed is fixed, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
Loudness depends on amplitude and on how far the sound has travelled, since energy spreads out.
Pitch depends on frequency and is not changed by the amplitude, so a louder note of the same pitch has the same frequency.
The frequency of a wave does not change when it passes from one medium to another, but the speed and the wavelength do.

items.text: A wave of frequency 250 Hz travels at 330 metres per second. Find its wavelength.
Find the frequency of a sound wave of wavelength 2 m travelling in air at 340 metres per second.

learn.title: Echo, reverberation and the audible range

blocks.text: Sound reflects from surfaces obeying the same laws as light. When a reflected sound is heard separately from the direct sound it is an echo, and this happens only when the reflected sound returns after a sufficient time gap for the ear to separate it. If the reflecting surfaces are close, the reflections overlap into a single lingering sound called reverberation.

items: The ear needs at least 0.1 second to distinguish a reflected sound from the direct sound, so an echo requires a time gap of at least 0.1 second.
Since the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, the minimum distance is v multiplied by 0.1 divided by 2, which is 17.2 m for a speed of 344 metres per second.
Reverberation occurs when the reflecting surfaces are nearer than about 17 m, so the sounds overlap and the original cannot be distinguished.
Curtains, carpets and rough surfaces absorb sound and reduce reverberation, while hard flat surfaces such as glass and tiles reflect it strongly.
Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound and sounds above 20000 Hz are ultrasound, neither of which can be heard by the average human ear.

items.text: How far from a reflecting wall must a person stand to hear an echo, taking the speed of sound as 344 metres per second?
items.note: The minimum time gap is 0.1 second. The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is v multiplied by t = 344 x 0.1 = 34.4 m. This is twice the distance from the wall, so the person must stand at least 34.4/2 = 17.2 m from the wall.

keyPoints: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and requires a material medium to travel.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
A sound wave is longitudinal, and the particles vibrate about fixed positions.
Sound travels fastest in a solid, then a liquid, and slowest in a gas.
Speed of sound in air is about 330 to 344 metres per second.
v = f lambda, so lambda = v/f and f = v/lambda.
Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive compressions.
Frequency is the number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency.
Frequency is unchanged when a wave moves between media, but speed and wavelength change.
An echo needs a time gap of at least 0.1 second.
Minimum echo distance = v x 0.1 / 2, which is 17.2 m at 344 metres per second.
Reverberation is the overlapping of reflections when surfaces are closer than about 17 m.
The audible range of the human ear is 20 Hz to 20000 Hz.
Soft surfaces absorb sound; hard surfaces reflect it.
examFocus: Echo questions must halve the distance, because the sound travels to the surface and back; using the full distance is the standard error.
v = f lambda requires the wavelength in metres, the frequency in hertz and the speed in metres per second, so convert before substituting.
Pitch and loudness must not be confused: changing amplitude changes loudness only, while changing frequency changes pitch only.
State the medium whenever giving the speed of sound, since the same frequency travels at a very different wavelength in air and in steel.
A question about sound in a vacuum is answered by the need for a medium, not by anything about amplitude or frequency.

vocabulary.meaning: The distance between two consecutive points in phase on a wave, such as two adjacent compressions.
The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
The maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its equilibrium position.
The sensation determined by frequency; higher frequency means higher pitch.
A distinctly heard reflection of sound, requiring a time gap of at least 0.1 second.
The overlapping of reflections in a confined space so that the original sound cannot be distinguished.

questions.prompt: Sound cannot travel through:
questions.answer: a vacuum
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles to carry the vibration, so without any medium there is nothing to transmit it. Light, being an electromagnetic wave, does travel through a vacuum.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing a gas, in which sound travels well, albeit more slowly than in a solid.

questions.prompt: A sound wave is an example of a:
questions.answer: longitudinal wave
questions.explanation: In sound the particles of the medium vibrate along the direction in which the wave travels, alternately compressing and rarefying the medium, which defines a longitudinal wave.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing transverse, which describes a wave on a stretched string where the particles oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel.

questions.prompt: Sound travels fastest through:
questions.answer: a solid
questions.explanation: The speed depends on how closely the particles are packed and on how quickly the disturbance is passed between them. In a solid the particles are closest and most rigidly linked, so sound travels fastest there, then in a liquid, and slowest in a gas.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing a vacuum, which transmits no sound at all rather than transmitting it quickly.

questions.prompt: The loudness of a sound depends on its:
questions.answer: amplitude
questions.explanation: A larger amplitude means the particles move further and transfer more energy, so the sound is louder. Wavelength and frequency together determine the pitch, not the loudness.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing frequency, which changes the pitch while leaving the loudness determined by amplitude.

questions.prompt: The minimum distance from a wall for an echo to be heard, taking the speed of sound as 344 metres per second, is:
questions.explanation: The time gap must be at least 0.1 second, so the sound travels 344 x 0.1 = 34.4 m in that time. This is the round trip, so the wall distance is half of it, 17.2 m.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 34.4 m, which is the total distance travelled by the sound rather than the distance to the wall.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the number of oscillations made by a source per second is called its ________.
questions.answer: frequency, measured in hertz
questions.explanation: One hertz is one oscillation per second, and the frequency determines the pitch of the sound produced.
questions.commonMistake: Answering amplitude, which describes how far the particles move and therefore how loud the sound is.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a sound wave with a frequency below 20 Hz is called ________ and cannot be heard by the human ear.
questions.answer: infrasound, whereas above 20000 Hz it is ultrasound
questions.explanation: The audible range of the average human ear is about 20 Hz to 20000 Hz, so sounds below it are infrasound and above it are ultrasound.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the two names, calling a very high frequency infrasound.

questions.prompt: Find the wavelength of a sound wave of frequency 250 Hz travelling in air at 330 metres per second.
questions.answer: From v = f lambda, the wavelength is lambda = v/f = 330/250 = 1.32 m.
questions.explanation: The speed and frequency are both given, so the wavelength follows directly by dividing them.
questions.commonMistake: Multiplying the speed by the frequency, which would give a dimensionally meaningless result.

questions.prompt: Find the frequency of a sound wave of wavelength 2 m travelling in air at 340 metres per second.
questions.answer: From v = f lambda, the frequency is f = v/lambda = 340/2 = 170 Hz.
questions.explanation: Rearranging the wave equation gives the frequency as the speed divided by the wavelength.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing the wavelength by the speed, which inverts the relationship.

questions.prompt: A sound wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.66 m. Find the speed of the wave and state through which medium it is most likely travelling.
questions.answer: From v = f lambda, the speed is 500 x 0.66 = 330 metres per second. A speed of about 330 metres per second is the speed of sound in air at ordinary temperature, so the wave is most likely travelling in air. A speed of this value is far too small for steel, where sound travels at about 5000 metres per second, and far too large for a vacuum, where sound does not travel at all.
questions.explanation: The speed identifies the medium, because the speed of sound differs greatly between air, water and solids.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the wave must be in a solid, since the formula does not reveal the medium on its own.

questions.prompt: A sound wave of frequency 200 Hz passes from air into water, in which its speed is 1500 metres per second while the speed in air is 350 metres per second. Find its wavelength in each medium.
questions.answer: In air, lambda = v/f = 350/200 = 1.75 m. In water, lambda = 1500/200 = 7.5 m. The frequency remains 200 Hz in both media because it is fixed by the source and the boundary between the media does not change the rate at which wavefronts arrive. Since the speed increases while the frequency stays constant, the wavelength increases in proportion, from 1.75 m to 7.5 m.
questions.explanation: Frequency is a property of the source and is unchanged at a boundary, so the whole change in speed appears as a change in wavelength.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping the wavelength the same and changing the frequency, which would contradict the fixed rate of arrival of wavefronts.

questions.prompt: Explain, with reasons, why a person standing in front of a cliff hears an echo after 2 seconds, taking the speed of sound as 340 metres per second, and find the distance to the cliff.
questions.answer: The time of 2 seconds is greater than the minimum 0.1 second needed for the reflected sound to be heard separately, so the reflection is perceived as a distinct echo rather than as reverberation. The sound travels to the cliff and back in that time, so the total distance travelled is 340 x 2 = 680 m. The distance to the cliff is half the total, so it is 680/2 = 340 m.
questions.explanation: The round trip must be halved to obtain the distance to the reflecting surface, and the time must exceed 0.1 second for an echo rather than reverberation.
questions.commonMistake: Reporting 680 m as the distance to the cliff, forgetting that the sound returns along the same path.

questions.prompt: The frequency of a sound wave is 50 Hz and its speed in air is 350 metres per second. Find its wavelength, and find the frequency of a wave travelling at the same frequency through steel of speed 5000 metres per second.
questions.answer: In air, lambda = v/f = 350/50 = 7 m. In steel the frequency is set by the source and is unchanged at 50 Hz, but the speed is 5000 metres per second, so the wavelength becomes lambda = v/f = 5000/50 = 100 m. The question asks for the frequency in steel, which remains 50 Hz, and the important consequence is the very large change in wavelength from 7 m to 100 m.
questions.explanation: A wave entering a denser medium becomes much longer, because the speed rises while the frequency is held fixed by the source.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the frequency rises in proportion to the speed, which would wrongly increase the pitch of the sound on entering steel.

questions.prompt: Explain why a bell cannot be heard inside a jar from which the air has been pumped out, and what this experiment demonstrates.
questions.answer: Sound is produced by the vibrating bell and is transmitted by the vibration of the particles of the surrounding medium. When the air is pumped out of the jar the vibrating bell and the medium separating it from the observer are removed, so there are too few particles to carry the disturbance to the outside and no sound is heard. The bell can still be seen vibrating, and the suspended gong inside the jar also fails to ring when struck, since there is no air to transmit the vibration to it. The experiment therefore demonstrates that a material medium is essential for the propagation of sound and that sound does not travel through a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Removing the medium removes the transmission path while leaving the vibration itself intact, isolating the medium as the necessary factor.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the bell stops vibrating, when the bell continues to vibrate and only the transmission of that vibration fails.

questions.prompt: Explain why sound is heard more clearly in a carpeted hall than in a hall with a bare tiled floor and glass windows, given the same sound produced at the same volume.
questions.answer: Hard flat surfaces such as glass, tiles and polished walls reflect sound very strongly, so a large fraction of the sound energy is returned to the listener by many different paths and at many different times. These overlapping reflections produce reverberation, in which the original sound is smeared out and masked by its own reflections, so consonants and the ends of syllables become difficult to distinguish. Soft materials such as carpets, curtains and upholstered seats absorb a large fraction of the incident sound, converting it to a small internal vibration rather than returning it to the room. With less reflected energy the direct sound is heard cleanly, which improves clarity without the source becoming louder.
questions.explanation: Clarity depends on the ratio of direct to reflected sound, and absorption raises that ratio by destroying the reflections.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the sound is quieter in the carpeted hall, when the total energy is comparable and only its distribution in time differs.

questions.prompt: State the audible range of the human ear and name the terms used for sounds above and below this range.
questions.answer: The audible range of the average human ear is about 20 Hz to 20000 Hz. Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound and sounds above 20000 Hz are called ultrasound. Infrasound is produced by elephants, whales and some volcanic activity, while ultrasound is used in medical imaging, in sonar and in cleaning jewellery.
questions.explanation: The audible range bounds what the average ear can detect, with named terms for the regions outside it.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the two terms, describing a frequency above 20000 Hz as infrasound.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between pitch and loudness, and state which of them changes if the amplitude of a sound wave is doubled while its frequency is unchanged.
questions.answer: Pitch is the sensation produced by frequency, so a higher frequency gives a higher pitch, while loudness is the sensation produced by amplitude and by the distance travelled, so a larger amplitude gives a louder sound. If the amplitude is doubled while the frequency is unchanged, the sound becomes louder but its pitch does not change at all. Since the frequency is unchanged and the speed in the medium is also unchanged, the wavelength lambda = v/f is unchanged as well.
questions.explanation: Amplitude and frequency control independent sensations, so changing one leaves the other untouched.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the pitch rises because the sound is louder, confusing the two sensations.

questions.prompt: How far from a wall must a person stand to hear an echo, taking the speed of sound as 350 metres per second?
questions.answer: The minimum time gap for a distinct echo is 0.1 second. In that time the sound travels 350 x 0.1 = 35 m. This is the round trip, so the distance from the wall is 35/2 = 17.5 m, and the person must stand at least that far away.
questions.explanation: The echo condition fixes the total path length, and the distance to the wall is half of it.
questions.commonMistake: Using 0.1 second as the time for the sound to reach the wall, forgetting the return journey.

questions.prompt: Two waves of the same frequency travel through air, one with amplitude 2 mm and the other with 8 mm. Compare their wavelengths, their speeds and their relative loudness.
questions.answer: The wavelengths are equal, because the wavelength depends only on the speed and the frequency, lambda = v/f, and both waves have the same frequency in the same medium with the same speed. The speeds are equal for the same reason. The loudness differs: the second wave has an amplitude four times greater, so it carries more energy and is louder. No numerical ratio of loudness is implied, since perceived loudness does not vary in simple proportion to amplitude.
questions.explanation: Amplitude affects only the energy carried and hence the loudness; wavelength and speed depend on frequency and the medium.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming the larger amplitude gives a longer wavelength, which confuses amplitude with wavelength.

questions.prompt: Why does the sound of an explosion travel more slowly through air on a cold winter morning than on a hot summer afternoon?
questions.answer: The speed of sound in air depends on the temperature of the air, and it is greater at higher temperatures. On a cold winter morning the air molecules are moving more slowly and are on average further apart, so a compression is passed from molecule to molecule more slowly, and the wave travels more slowly. On a hot summer afternoon the molecules move more quickly and are closer together, so the disturbance is transmitted faster. This difference is also the reason that refraction of sound in air can make a sound audible over distances that would otherwise be beyond the direct line of sight.
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave, so its speed is set by how rapidly the medium's particles transmit the disturbance, which rises with temperature.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the cold air is denser so the sound is blocked, confusing density effects in a solid with temperature effects in a gas.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a longitudinal wave and give one example of each of a longitudinal and a transverse wave.
questions.answer: A longitudinal wave is one in which the particles of the medium oscillate along the same line as the direction in which the wave travels, producing regions of compression and rarefaction. Sound in air and in a liquid is longitudinal. A transverse wave is one in which the particles oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel; a wave on a stretched string or a ripple on the surface of water are examples.
questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature is the direction of particle motion relative to the direction of energy travel.
questions.commonMistake: Giving light as a transverse wave example, since light is electromagnetic and involves no particles of a medium at all.

questions.prompt: Find the time taken for sound to travel 1650 m in air at a speed of 330 metres per second, and state how this time changes if the sound then enters water at 1500 metres per second for the same distance.
questions.answer: In air, the time is distance divided by speed, so 1650/330 = 5 seconds. In water, where the speed is 1500 metres per second, the same distance takes 1650/1500 = 1.1 seconds. The time is therefore shorter in water, because the sound moves faster through the more densely packed particles of a liquid.
questions.explanation: Time is inversely proportional to speed for a fixed distance, so a faster medium gives a shorter travel time.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping the time the same in both media, assuming the distance fixes the time.

questions.prompt: The distance between two consecutive compressions in a sound wave is 2.5 cm. Find the frequency of the sound if its speed in air is 340 metres per second.
questions.answer: The distance between consecutive compressions is the wavelength, so lambda = 2.5 cm = 0.025 m. The frequency is f = v/lambda = 340/0.025 = 13600 Hz, that is 13.6 kHz. This lies within the audible range of the human ear, which extends to about 20000 Hz, so the sound can be heard.
questions.explanation: The spacing of compressions is the wavelength, which must be converted to metres before dividing the speed by it.
questions.commonMistake: Using 2.5 as though it were already in metres, which would give a frequency 100 times too large.

questions.prompt: Explain why the energy of a sound wave decreases as it travels away from the source, and why the sound may become inaudible at a distance.
questions.answer: The energy of a sound wave spreads out as the wave travels, because the same energy passes through a progressively larger surface area at increasing distance. The intensity, which is the energy passing through unit area per second, therefore decreases as the inverse square of the distance, so at four times the distance the intensity is one sixteenth. A further fraction of the energy is converted to heat by friction and viscosity as the sound moves through the medium, and it is absorbed particularly well by soft materials. Once the intensity falls below the threshold of hearing of the ear, which is about 10 to the power minus 12 watts per square metre, the sound is no longer perceived even though a very small amount of energy is still arriving.
questions.explanation: Spreading over a larger area and conversion to heat both reduce the intensity until it drops below the threshold of hearing.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the sound has run out of energy entirely at the limit of audibility, rather than having fallen below the threshold of the ear.

questions.prompt: Why are soft furnishings such as curtains and carpets used in concert halls?
questions.answer: Soft furnishings absorb sound rather than reflecting it, since their rough and porous surfaces convert much of the incident sound energy into internal vibrations and heat. This reduces the amount of reflected sound and therefore reduces reverberation in the hall, so the direct sound from the musicians reaches the audience clearly without being masked by overlapping echoes. They also help to prevent sound from escaping through windows and doors, improving the audibility for everyone in the audience.
questions.explanation: Absorbing materials reduce reverberation, which is what causes the original sound to be masked by its own reflections.
questions.commonMistake: Saying they make the hall quieter overall, when the purpose is to improve clarity of the sound that is produced.

questions.prompt: A sounding bell is suspended in a hall and a person at the far wall hears the bell directly but not an echo. The hall is 16 m long and the speed of sound is 340 metres per second. Explain why no echo is heard.
questions.answer: For a distinct echo the reflected sound must return at least 0.1 second after the direct sound, otherwise the two are heard as one prolonged sound. The sound travels to the far wall and back, a total distance of 2 x 16 = 32 m, so the time taken is 32/340 = 0.094 seconds. This is less than 0.1 second, so the reflected sound arrives too quickly after the direct sound for the ear to separate the two, and the listener hears a single sustained note instead. The hall is therefore too small for an echo to be heard, even though the walls do reflect sound.
questions.explanation: The condition for an echo is a time gap of at least 0.1 second. The round trip in a 16 m hall takes 32/340 = 0.094 seconds, which falls short of that gap, so the reflection is heard as part of the same sound rather than as a separate echo. The walls do reflect the sound; the hall is simply too small for the ear to separate the two.
questions.commonMistake: Stating that sound is not reflected because the hall is small, or forgetting that the distance to be halved is the round trip and not the one-way distance.
